public_content.story:
At A Pet’s Place Animal Hospital, caring for pets also means building relationships with the people who love them. Located on Coffman Street in Longmont, the hospital focuses on personalized veterinary care, helping families understand their pets’ needs and make informed decisions throughout every stage of life.

The people behind the practice bring lifelong connections with animals to their work. Managing veterinarian Dr. Jenelle Vail grew up in Colorado caring for horses, farm animals, and injured wildlife before pursuing veterinary medicine and working in animal shelter care. That background informs her interest in helping new puppy and kitten owners, managing complex medical needs, and supporting senior pets’ comfort and quality of life.

The hospital’s approach combines veterinary care with owner education and ongoing support. From preventive visits to times when a pet needs additional attention, the team aims to develop lasting relationships with Longmont families—getting to know both the animals in their care and the people beside them.

name: Ambrosia Glass Art
description: A Longmont glassblowing studio creating fine glass art and custom work while offering private lessons, two-person workshops and group glassblowing experiences for a range of skill levels.

public_content.name: Ambrosia Glass Art
public_content.story:
Behind Ambrosia Glass Art is Angelo Ambrosia, whose creative journey began with lessons from his father, Alphonse. Woodworking, photography, and black-and-white film processing introduced him to the care and craftsmanship involved in making something beautiful. Those early experiences sparked a fascination with creating that would carry him through several art forms.

As a young man, Angelo discovered clay, learning to work on the pottery wheel and shape simple vessels. While attending college in Prescott, Arizona, he continued developing his ideas through functional pottery and one-of-a-kind pieces. His next chapter took him to Lopez Island, Washington, where he worked with clay and stone to build kilns, fireplaces, and buildings while experimenting with firing techniques and new forms.

In 1999, Angelo moved to Santa Fe, New Mexico, producing ceramic art for retail and wholesale markets. He also collaborated with other artists and craftspeople on large public art projects in the surrounding area.

After several years in Santa Fe, Angelo settled in Longmont, where he discovered glassblowing—the art form that became his lasting passion. His work brings together the curiosity developed throughout his creative life and his belief that functional and sculptural art should express emotion, creativity, and craftsmanship. Today, Angelo’s work is available directly from the artist and through local and national galleries.

name: Barbed Wire Books
description: An independently owned downtown bookstore selling new and used books. Browse Colorado and local-interest titles, hard-to-find books, maps and guides, plus work from local authors and craftspeople.

public_content.name: Barbed Wire Books
public_content.story:
Barbed Wire Books: A New Beginning That Became Part of Longmont’s Story

At 504 Main Street in downtown Longmont, Barbed Wire Books brings together new releases, well-loved used books, Colorado history, and the pleasure of finding something unexpected. Behind its shelves is a story of starting over—and a lifelong connection to books that owner Kathe Heinecken turned into a business in 2009.

When Kathe opened the store, she was navigating the end of a 25-year marriage, working three jobs, and preparing for her son to enter college. The economy was struggling, but she believed in her abilities and saw a need for a bookstore in Longmont. In a later interview with ShoutOut Colorado, she described opening Barbed Wire Books as a step toward a different future. Its name reflected something personal, too: her appreciation for the West and the ranching way of life.

Books had been part of Kathe’s life long before she became a business owner. At 14, she worked in a bookstore wrapping Christmas purchases. Her path later included construction and hauling lumber in a semi truck, with a book beside her on the passenger seat. After becoming a mother, she volunteered in schools and worked with gifted children, encouraging reading and writing. Library volunteering and several years working in a used bookstore added to the experience she brought to her own shop.

Today, Barbed Wire Books offers readers many ways to explore. Its new-book section includes fiction, nonfiction, bestsellers, and a dedicated selection of pop-up books. The used shelves change as books arrive through customer trades. Colorado titles and Western Americana give the store a strong connection to its surroundings, alongside maps and guides covering local landscapes, wildlife, geology, and places to visit. Gifts, bookmarks, jewelry, and cards offer smaller discoveries along the way.

Personal service remains central to the experience. Staff can help readers locate out-of-print titles, arrange special orders, appraise collectible books, or build a collection. Customers searching for a used title can also place a reserve request, allowing the store to contact them if a copy comes in through trade. Accepted gently used books earn credit toward eligible used inventory, giving those books another opportunity to find a reader.

The store’s history also includes people sharing their own stories. Its event archive documents book clubs, author events, novel-writing gatherings, poetry performances, and open mic nights. These past gatherings show the role Barbed Wire Books has played as a meeting place for readers and writers. Its classroom reading-list program adds another connection, helping local schools arrange new and used copies for students.

Even the front window has a personality. Barb Dwyer, the store’s playful spokesperson and muse, appears in themed displays ranging from handicrafts to construction and writing. The website’s gallery preserves years of these imaginative scenes—a small Main Street tradition that gives passersby a reason to pause.

Readers farther away can support the shop through its online partnerships with Bookshop.org, Libro.fm, and Biblio, covering new books, digital audiobooks, and rare or collectible titles. But for anyone exploring downtown Longmont, the shelves at Barbed Wire Books offer an invitation to spend a little time browsing—and perhaps leave with a story they had not planned to find.
public_content.description: An independently owned downtown bookstore selling new and used books. Browse Colorado and local-interest titles, hard-to-find books, maps and guides, plus work from local authors and craftspeople.

name: Brickscape Cafe
description: Longmont's award-winning LEGO-themed cafe and toy store with a wide selection of coffee, loose-leaf tea, smoothies, lemonade, soda, and new and used LEGO sets.

public_content.name: Brickscape Cafe
public_content.story:
Brickscape Café: The Longmont Gathering Place Built Around Play

Brickscape Café began with a few folding tables, LEGO® bricks, themed beverages, and an idea: building together could help people connect. From its beginnings as a pop-up in 2022, it grew into a distinctive Longmont business combining a toy shop, makerspace, and café.

Founder Billie Abbitt’s vision extended beyond selling building sets. Brickscape offered a place where children, parents, grandparents, and adults visiting on their own could share an activity, explore their creativity, and find company.

From Pop-Up Tables to a Storefront

Brickscape opened its first physical store in March 2023 at Old Town Marketplace, at 332 Main Street. Early offerings included new and used LEGO sets, retired sets, minifigures, and small gifts. Despite its name, the business did not yet have the space for a full café.

In a May 2023 Westword interview, Abbitt described bringing together two interests: the community atmosphere of a coffee shop previously operated in Gainesville, Florida, and the creative possibilities of LEGO building. Sorting and building with the family’s bricks had become a meaningful personal activity, helping inspire the business.

Early programming included a mindfulness workshop with local nonprofit SunShineBlu and themed LEGO engineering camps. The store was already developing into a place for shared experiences as well as shopping.

A Growing Place to Gather

Brickscape expanded beyond its original retail space, eventually operating at 900 Coffman Street, Suite C, in the plaza with Your Butcher Frank. The larger location brought together retail shelves, building tables, a makerspace, and a full coffee and smoothie bar.

Visitors could browse LEGO sets and gifts, rent selected sets, or work with loose bricks in the open-build area. Espresso drinks, teas, smoothies, and snacks helped make the space a place to linger.

Its open-build program used a pay-what-it’s-worth approach rather than a fixed hourly admission charge. Guests contributed according to their experience and circumstances, helping support brick cleaning, supplies, and continued access.

Birthday celebrations, story times, camps, puzzle nights, and workshops offered different ways to participate. Brickscape also advertised school fundraiser nights, contributing a portion of qualifying café sales to participating schools.

Recognition From the Community

Brickscape’s combination of shopping, hospitality, and creative play earned recognition across several categories.

Its website’s account of the 2025 Times-Call Best of Longmont awards identified wins for Best Gift Shop, Best Makerspace, and Best Toy Store. A later announcement on Brickscape’s LinkedIn page reported five CommunityVotes honors: Platinum recognition for Children’s Activities, Child Play Places, Hobby, Toy and Game Stores, and Toys, plus Gold for Cafés and Coffee Shops.

In the founder’s farewell announcement, Brickscape reported cumulative totals of six Best of Longmont awards and eight CommunityVotes awards, along with a sixth-place Colorado toy-store ranking from BusinessRate.

Community Connections

Brickscape’s public programs reached beyond its everyday customers. The founder’s farewell described partnerships with local schools, the City of Longmont, the museum, library, and community organizations. Those connections helped welcome foster families, neurodiverse participants, people with developmental disabilities, and seniors.

The common activity was simple: sit down, choose some bricks, and build. Participants did not need to arrive with the same interests, experience, or finished project in mind.

The Closure Announcement—and an Uncertain Next Chapter

In a message posted on Brickscape’s website, Abbitt announced October 14 as the café’s last day. The message explained that personal circumstances left insufficient time and energy to lead a proposed transition into a nonprofit.

The announcement did not settle whether Brickscape might eventually reopen, continue in another form, or offer camps elsewhere.

Community members also organized a “Save Brickscape Cafe” fundraising campaign. Its organizers described an effort to support operating costs and develop a community-led nonprofit future. That campaign represents a proposed next chapter, rather than confirmation that a transition has been completed.

Whatever follows, Brickscape has earned a place in Longmont’s local business history. Its story records how a pop-up grew into an award-winning gathering space—and how a familiar toy became the starting point for friendships, family activities, and a community’s effort to keep a valued place alive.

name: Recovery Café Longmont
description: A community-centered recovery organization creating a welcoming space for people rebuilding their lives. Volunteer opportunities include cooking, hospitality, teaching classes and helping with support activities.

public_content.name: Recovery Café Longmont
public_content.story:
Recovery Café Longmont: A Place to Belong, Connect, and Begin Again

Recovery Café Longmont grew from a community recognizing a need—and choosing to respond with compassion. In 2018, leadership at CENTRALongmont Presbyterian Church began exploring how to create a welcoming place for people navigating recovery. That effort connected them with the Recovery Café Network, and in 2019, Recovery Café Longmont opened its doors. The Café operates as an independent organization and is not faith-based, welcoming people from all backgrounds.

At its heart is the belief that every person deserves dignity, connection, and an opportunity to grow. Located in downtown Longmont, the Café supports adults recovering from substance use, mental health challenges, trauma, isolation, and other difficult life experiences. It offers a consistent community where people can build relationships and find encouragement through the ongoing work of rebuilding their lives.

That mission takes shape in everyday moments: sharing a meal, checking in with peers, learning something new, or celebrating a personal milestone. Members participate in weekly Recovery Circles, where they can discuss challenges, recognize progress, and work toward goals. School for Recovery classes offer opportunities to explore art, music, storytelling, yoga, and other tools for growth. Members can also receive help finding resources for housing, employment, food security, treatment, and mental health support. 

Behind this work is a team that brings together professional knowledge, community involvement, and personal experience with recovery. Executive Director Dr. Waltrina DeFrantz-Dufor contributes more than 30 years of higher education and nonprofit leadership experience. Alongside her, peer support specialists, program staff, volunteers, and board members help create a dependable, caring environment. The team’s work includes bilingual outreach and recovery navigation, extending support to people facing barriers to connection and essential services. 

Members also help shape the community they join. Contributing to Café life is part of membership, giving people opportunities to share their strengths and support one another. This spirit of mutual care makes Recovery Café Longmont a place where people can both receive encouragement and discover what they have to offer. 

For Longmont, the Café offers something deeply valuable: a continuing place of welcome, where recovery is supported through relationships, respect, and the chance to keep moving forward together. 

Learn about membership, volunteering, and ways to support the Café at [recoverycafelongmont.org](https://recoverycafelongmont.org/).

description: An Old Town Longmont micro-bakery centered on artisan sourdough, baked goods and hands-on sourdough workshops, with preorder-based local pickup.

public_content.name: Salt and Bread
public_content.story:
**Salt and Bread: A Love of Baking, Shared with Longmont**

For Bethany, the founder of Salt and Bread, the kitchen has always been a place of connection. Feeding people brings her joy, and that love of bringing others together eventually grew into a microbakery rooted in Old Town Longmont.

Her journey into sourdough began after a decade of eating gluten free. Discovering the traditional breadmaking process sparked a fascination that kept growing: a single loaf became several, and baking at home became a vision of sharing bread with her neighborhood. Salt and Bread grew from that combination of curiosity, craftsmanship, and care for the community.

Today, that same spirit extends to helping others experience the satisfaction of baking for themselves. Salt and Bread approaches sourdough as a skill that can fit into everyday life, with practical guidance and an invitation to slow down and enjoy making something by hand.

The Salt and Bread Sourdough Kit brings together baking tools, dehydrated starter, ingredients for a first loaf, and a digital recipe book. From a proofing basket to tools for shaping and scoring dough, its contents help give beginning bakers a place to start.

For those who already have their tools, the downloadable Sourdough Guide offers instructions for bread, pizza crust, cinnamon rolls, and brown butter chocolate chip cookies. Photography and journal prompts accompany the recipes, encouraging bakers to develop a routine that feels personal and manageable.

Bethany also welcomes inquiries about private workshops and special requests. Her newsletter carries the conversation beyond the mixing bowl through kitchen stories, recipes, and encouragement to make room for slower moments. Together, these offerings reflect the idea at the heart of Salt and Bread: something as simple as making bread can become a meaningful way to create, share, and connect.

Explore their offerings at [saltandbreadco.com](https://www.saltandbreadco.com/).
public_content.description: An Old Town Longmont micro-bakery centered on artisan sourdough, baked goods and hands-on sourdough workshops, with preorder-based local pickup.

name: Shoes & Brews
description: A distinctly Longmont combination of specialty running store and taproom, pairing running shoes and gear with community runs, local beer and a social gathering place for runners and walkers.

public_content.name: Shoes & Brews
public_content.story:
Shoes & Brews: Bringing Longmont Together, One Step at a Time

Shoes & Brews began with an idea shared among friends: combine a love of running with the friendships that grow over a post-run beer. In 2014, Ashlee Anderson, Colin Anderson, and their friend Dave Zakavec, joined by family members, brought that idea to life in Longmont. They created a place where finding the right running shoes and spending time with neighbors could happen under the same roof.

The shoe store supports people with different goals, whether they are training for a race, enjoying daily walks, or looking for more comfortable footwear. Alongside shoes, customers can browse running apparel, nutrition, and accessories, with staff helping them choose equipment suited to their needs. That practical focus makes the shop useful to experienced runners and people just getting started.

The taproom adds another reason to stay awhile. Shoes & Brews makes small batches of its own beer on a one-barrel brewing system and serves them alongside rotating guest selections. Its beverage offerings also include cider, wine, and nonalcoholic options. With a patio, games, and a setting that welcomes children and dogs, the gathering space reaches beyond the running community.

Community runs bring those two sides of the business together. The year-round Thursday run club gives people a regular opportunity to get moving and connect, while the events calendar includes gatherings such as trivia, live music, and visits from running brands. These activities give residents and visitors different ways to become part of the Shoes & Brews community.

One of its most distinctive traditions is the 800-Meter Challenge, which connects a runner’s finishing time to the price of a beer. It is a playful expression of the idea behind the business: running and socializing can share the same finish line.

At its heart, Shoes & Brews offers a welcoming place to find your fit—in a pair of shoes, among fellow runners, or around a taproom table. You can come for footwear, a drink, or conversation; the business welcomes people who enjoy either side of its personality, as well as those who appreciate both.
public_content.address: 63 S. Pratt Pkwy., Unit B Longmont, CO 80501

name: SNOW Apparel
description: An independent downtown women's boutique focused on slow fashion, with clothing and accessories selected around quality, ethical production and sustainable materials.

public_content.name: SNOW Apparel
public_content.story:
SNOW Apparel: Thoughtful Fashion with a Personal Purpose

SNOW Apparel’s story began with a decision to build a different kind of boutique. In 2013, while developing her business plan, founder Snow learned of the devastating garment-building collapse in Bangladesh. The tragedy changed how she wanted to approach fashion and the business she hoped to create.

She spent the following years researching clothing companies and reshaping her plans around craftsmanship, responsible production, and lasting quality. Along the way, she discovered independent designers and small, family-run businesses throughout the United States and Canada whose values aligned with her own.

In 2017, SNOW Apparel opened its doors. Today, the downtown Longmont women’s boutique brings that vision to life through a carefully selected collection of clothing and accessories. Its approach embraces slow fashion, with styles ranging from classic and timeless to playful and whimsical.

Customer stories featured on the boutique’s website highlight Snow’s attentive service, enthusiasm, and help finding flattering styles. That personal connection complements the purpose behind her selections: encouraging shoppers to consider both what they enjoy wearing and the people who make it.

Visit SNOW Apparel at 520 Main Street, Suite B-1, or explore [snowapparel.us](https://snowapparel.us/).
